title: Disruption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz

charter.in: The disruption of commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz that began when Iran's Revolutionary Guards declared the strait closed after the US-Israeli strikes on Iran of 28 February 2026. Stories belong when they report on passage through the strait itself: traffic levels, closures and reopenings, attacks on or seizures of merchant ships in and near the strait, stranded ships and crews, insurance, escorts, US and Iranian blockades of the strait's traffic, tolls and permit rules, and deals, talks or decisions about passage.
out: The wider US/Israel–Iran war: air and missile strikes, battles and casualties that do not concern shipping
US–Iran ceasefire and peace talks, except where the story is about terms for passage through the strait
Iran's nuclear program, enrichment and inspections
Oil, gas and fuel prices and markets, IEA reserve releases, OPEC+ output
Energy and fertilizer security and shortages in importing countries
Houthi threats and shipping in the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb
US sanctions on Iran's oil revenue and finance, and the US land blockade ('Iron Gate')
Pre-war naval drills and the military standoff around the strait in February 2026
charter.endEvent: Commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz returns to roughly pre-war levels, with Iran's closure, permit and toll regime and the US naval blockade lifted (a lasting reopening, not a truce-day pause).

figures.name: Traffic below pre-war normal
figures.definition: How far commercial vessel transits through the Strait of Hormuz (all ship types) are below pre-war levels, as a percentage. A level at the time stated, not cumulative. A value stated as a share of normal (e.g. "fallen to roughly 5%") is recorded as the drop (95).
variants: oil shipments through the strait (e.g. "under 10 percent of pre-war levels")

figures.name: Ships stranded
figures.definition: Merchant ships trapped in the Gulf or otherwise unable to transit the Strait of Hormuz because of the closure, at the time stated. A stock, not cumulative. Seafarer counts (20,000; 11,000) are people, not this figure, and are not recorded.

figures.name: Daily transits
figures.definition: Commercial vessels crossing the Strait of Hormuz in a single day, from ship tracking. Our stories give the pre-war baseline as 100+ to about 130–140 a day; baselines are not recorded as values.
variants: ships counted crossing over several days (e.g. "nine since Monday")
vessels allowed through in one batch (e.g. "about two dozen")

notes: Boundary: entries report on passage through the strait itself. Optional entries are mainly about something else (war strikes, ultimatums, ceasefire talks, oil markets) but carry a substantive passage on the strait: a traffic figure, stranded ships, insurance, or a threat or strike whose stated purpose is reopening the strait or protecting ships in it. War, nuclear, price and Lebanon stories that only recap the closure in a clause are left out; the 15 most tempting are near misses. Start: the development begins with the 1 March IRGC "de facto closed" declaration. The 23 February explainer on drills that temporarily closed parts of the corridor is optional as a precursor; February drill and standoff stories are out. Same-event clusters: 13 and 14 April (US blockade order), 4 and 5 May (Project Freedom launch and first escorts) and 18 June (three stories on the deal reopening the strait). The earliest-published story of each event is marked as the turning point and the later same-event stories are routine; another story from the same cluster is an equally valid turning point. The 26 September offer and its 27 September rejection are two events and both are turning points. Our stories contradict each other on the 11 April reopening: "iran-proposes-paid-passage-for-oil-and-gas-ships" says Iran reopened the strait under the truce, while "us-and-iran-meet-as-oil-disruption-roils-markets" (same day) says the truce halted strikes "but not Iran’s blockade". The 19 April story confirms a brief reopening. Stranded ships disagree: about 2,000 ships (1 and 3 April, 24 May) versus more than 600 (13 April) and 900+ (4 May), with the same 20,000 seafarers cited for both 2,000 and 600 ships. Earlier counts (400+ vessels on 12 March, about 500 tankers on 18 March) are smaller and partly tankers only. Traffic disagrees too: "us-strikes-iran-as-shipping-falls-by-90" (6 November) says transits are down more than 90% since February, while six days later two stories citing UKMTO put traffic about 65% below prewar. "us-and-israel-prepare-for-renewed-strikes" (25 October) says Middle East oil exports have returned to pre-war levels and "iran-charges-ships-to-cross-the-world-s-key-oil-route" (7 November) puts Gulf exports at about 86% of pre-war: those count oil exports (partly via bypass routes), not transits, so they are not recorded as traffic values. Early traffic values (10, 12 and 29 March) count tanker traffic only and are marked matches false. "iran-tactics-paralyze-asian-oil-and-gas-flows" (12 May) gives the 95% collapse "within weeks" of the start; asOf is the story date because the text gives no date. Daily transits: "shipping-cuts-push-fuel-prices-and-food-costs-higher" gives a range ("as few as two to 16"), recorded as under 16. "u-s-will-keep-ships-to-halt-iran-oil-transit" (14 August) says transits fell "to single digits", which is not a number and is not recorded. Not tracked: oil flows lost (8–20 million barrels a day) appear mostly in energy-market near misses and in entries with inconsistent definitions; counts of ships attacked use different windows (about 20 vessels by 12 March, over 30 by 23 July, at least 27 in October, five in 48 hours). Tolls range from $1 a barrel to $2 million per vessel; Trump’s 20% fee on strait cargo (16 July) is reported only once. Open on 16 November 2026: no story reports the end event; the 14 November story still has traffic about 65% below normal. ROLES: entries with `eitherRole` accept either verdict, and the 16 July entry became a turning point (decision); each says why in `roleReview` (an AI session's review of 2026-11-22, not yet checked by a person). Blockade enforcement, analyses and UN appeals that repeat the known state stay routine.
